danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: Samme nat var Rostov med en deling på forpostkommando foran Bagrations afdeling. Hans husarer var placeret langs linjen parvis, og han selv red langs linjen og forsøgte at beherske den søvnighed, der stadigt overmandede ham. Et enormt rum, med vores hærs lejrbål svagt glødende i tågen, kunne anes bag ham; foran ham var tåget mørke. Rostov kunne intet se, hvor indtrængende han end stirrede ud i den tågede fjernhed: snart skimtede noget gråt, snart var der noget sort, snart syntes små lys at glimte, hvor fjenden burde være, snart troede han, det bare var noget i hans egne øjne. Hans øjne lukkede sig hele tiden, og i hans fantasi dukkede snart kejseren op, snart Denisov, snart minder fra Moskva — og han åbnede hastigt øjnene igen og så tæt foran sig hovedet og ørerne på den hest, han red, og sommetider, når han kom inden for seks skridt, husarernes sorte skikkelser; men i det fjerne var der stadig det samme tågede mørke. »Hvorfor ikke? ... Det kunne sagtens ske,« tænkte Rostov, »at kejseren møder mig og giver mig en ordre, som han ville give enhver anden officer; han vil sige: 'Rid ud og find ud af, hvad der er derovre.' Der findes mange historier om, at han har lært en officer at kende netop på den tilfældige måde og knyttet ham til sig! Tænk, hvis han gav mig en plads hos sig! Åh, jeg ville beskytte ham, jeg ville fortælle ham sandheden, jeg ville afsløre hans bedragere!« Og for levende at forestille sig sin hengivne kærlighed til kejseren forestillede Rostov sig en fjende eller en svigefuld tysker, som han ikke blot med glæde ville dræbe, men give en lussing foran kejserens øjne. Pludselig vækkede et fjernt råb ham. Han for sammen og slog øjnene op.

»Hvor er jeg? Åh ja, på forpostkæden ... feltraab og parole — skaft, Olmütz. Sikke en ærgrelse, at vores eskadron er i reserven i morgen,« tænkte han. »Jeg beder om orlov til at komme op til fronten, dette kan være min eneste chance for at se kejseren. Det varer ikke længe, før jeg er af vagt. Jeg tager en runde til, og når jeg kommer tilbage, går jeg til generalen og spørger.« Han rettede sig i sadlen og satte hesten i gang for endnu en gang at ride rundt om sine husarer. Det syntes ham, som om det blev lysere. Til venstre så han en skrånende nedkørsel belyst af noget, og over for den en sort knold, der syntes stejl som en mur. På den knold var der en hvid plet, som Rostov slet ikke kunne gøre rede for: var det en lysning i skoven belyst af månen, eller noget usmeltet sne, eller hvide huse? Han syntes endda, der bevægede sig noget på den hvide plet. »Det er nok sne ... den plet ... en plet — une tache,« tænkte han. »Nej, det er ikke en tache ... Natasja ... søster, sorte øjne ... Na... tasja... (Tænk, hvor hun vil blive overrasket, når jeg fortæller hende, at jeg har set kejseren!) Natasja ... tag min sabeltaske ...« — »Hold til højre, Deres nåde, der er buske her,« lød stemmen fra en husar, som Rostov red forbi i det øjeblik, han var ved at falde i søvn. Rostov løftede hovedet, der var sunket næsten ned til hestens manke, og standsede ved husaren. Han var ved at bukke under for en uimodståelig, ungdommelig, barnlig døsighed. »Men hvad tænkte jeg på? Jeg må ikke glemme det. Hvordan skal jeg tale til kejseren? Nej, det er ikke det — det er i morgen. Åh ja! Natasja ... sabeltaske ... sabler dem ned ... Hvem? Husarerne ... Ah, husarerne med overskæg. Ad Tverskaja-gaden red husaren med overskæg ... Jeg tænkte også på ham, lige over for Gurjevs hus ... Gamle Gurjev ... Ah, men Denisov er en fin fyr. Men det er alt sammen vrøvl. Det vigtigste er, at kejseren er her. Hvordan han så på mig og ønskede at sige noget, men ikke turde... Nej, det var mig, der ikke turde. Men det er vrøvl, det vigtigste er ikke at glemme den vigtige ting, jeg tænkte på. Ja, Na-tasja, sabeltaske, ah ja, ja! Det er rigtigt!« Og hans hoved sank igen mod hestens hals. Med ét syntes han, at der blev skudt mod ham. »Hvad? Hvad? Hvad?... Hug dem ned! Hvad?...« sagde Rostov og vågnede. I det øjeblik han slog øjnene op, hørte han foran sig, hvor fjenden var, de langtrukne råb af tusinder af stemmer. Hans hest og husarens hest ved siden af spidsede ører ved de råb. Derovre, hvor råbene kom fra, flammede et bål op og slukkedes igen, så et andet, og langs hele den franske linje på bakken flammede bål op, og råbene voksede sig højere og højere. Rostov kunne høre lyden af franske ord, men kunne ikke skelne dem. Larm af mange stemmer var for stor; alt, hvad han kunne høre, var: »Ahahah!« og »rrrr!«
»Hvad er det? Hvad tror du?« sagde Rostov til husaren ved sin side. »Det må være fjendens lejr!«
Husaren svarede ikke.
»Nå, hører du det ikke?« spurgte Rostov igen efter at have ventet på svar.
»Hvem kan vide, Deres nåde?« svarede husaren modvilligt.
»Ud fra retningen at dømme må det være fjenden,« gentog Rostov.
»Det kan det være, eller det kan det ikke,« mumlede husaren. »Det er mørkt ... Stille!« hviskede han til sin urolige hest.

Rostovs hest var også urolig; den skrabede i den frosne jord, spidsede ører mod støjen og så hen mod lysene. Råbene voksede endnu højere og smeltede sammen til en brølen, som kun en hær af adskillige tusinde mand kunne frembringe. Lysene bredte sig længere og længere ud, sandsynligvis langs den franske lejrlinje. Rostov havde ikke længere lyst til at sove. Det fjendtlige hærs glade, triumferende råb virkede stimulerende på ham. »Vive l'Empereur! l'Empereur!« hørte han nu tydeligt.
»De kan ikke være langt borte, formodentlig lige hinsides åen,« sagde han til husaren ved sin side.

Husaren sukkede blot uden at svare og hostede irriteret. Lyden af hestetramp i trav langs husarlinjen hørtes, og ud af det tågede mørke dukkede skikkelsen af en husarsergeant pludselig op, kæmpestor som en elefant.
»Deres nåde, generalerne!« sagde sergeanten og red op til Rostov.

Rostov, der stadig så hen mod ildskinnet og råbene, red med sergeanten hen for at møde nogle ryttere, der kom ridende langs linjen. Den ene var på en hvid hest. Fyrst Bagration og fyrst Dolgorukov var med deres adjudanter kommet for at overvære det mærkelige fænomen med lys og råb i fjendens lejr. Rostov red hen til Bagration, rapporterede til ham og sluttede sig derpå til adjudanterne for at lytte til, hvad generalerne sagde.
»Tro mig,« sagde fyrst Dolgorukov henvendt til Bagration, »det er ikke andet end et trick! Han har trukket sig tilbage og beordret bagtroppen at tænde bål og larme for at narre os.«

»Det er ikke sandsynligt,« sagde Bagration. »Jeg så dem i aften på den knold; hvis de havde trukket sig tilbage, ville de også have forladt den... Officer!« sagde Bagration til Rostov, »er fjendens forposter stadig derude?«
»De var der i aften, men nu ved jeg det ikke, Deres eksellence. Skal jeg ride ud med nogle af mine husarer og se efter?« svarede Rostov.
Bagration standsede og forsøgte, inden han svarede, at se Rostovs ansigt i tågen.
»Gør det,« sagde han efter en pause.
»Ja, Deres eksellence.«

Rostov sporede sin hest, kaldte på sergeant Fedtjenko og to andre husarer, sagde dem at følge sig, og red i trav nedad bakken i den retning, råbene kom fra. Han følte sig både bange og glad over at ride alene med tre husarer ind i det mystiske og farlige tågede fjerne, hvor ingen havde været før ham. Bagration råbte efter ham fra bakken, at han ikke måtte ride over åen, men Rostov lod, som om han ikke hørte det, og standsede ikke, men red videre og videre og forvekslede hele tiden buske med træer og grøfter med mennesker og opdagede hele tiden sine fejltagelser. Da han var redet ned ad bakken i trav, kunne han hverken se vores egne eller fjendens bål, men han hørte franskmændenes råb højere og tydeligere. I dalen så han foran sig noget, der lignede en flod, men da han nåede det, opdagede han, at det var en vej. Da han var kommet ud på vejen, holdt han sin hest an og tøvede, om han skulle ride langs den eller krydse den og ride op ad bakken over den sorte mark. At holde sig til vejen, der skinnede hvidt i tågen, ville have været sikrere, fordi det var lettere at se folk komme. »Følg mig!« sagde han, krydsede vejen og begyndte at ride i galop op ad bakken mod det sted, hvor de franske forposter havde stået om aftenen.

»Deres nåde, der er han!« råbte en af husarerne bag ham. Og inden Rostov nåede at se, hvad den sorte ting var, der pludselig var dukket op i tågen, kom et glimt, fulgt af et skud, og en kugle, der susede højt oppe i tågen med en klagende lyd, forsvandt ud af hørevidde. Endnu et gevær brændte fejl, men glimtede i fænghullet. Rostov vendte sin hest og galopperede tilbage. Fire skud mere fulgte med mellemrum, og kuglerne fløj et sted i tågen og sang i forskellige toner. Rostov holdt sin hest an, der var blevet lige så oplivet som han selv af skydningen, og red tilbage i skridt. »Nå, bare lidt mere! Lidt mere!« sagde en munter stemme i hans sjæl. Men der kom ikke flere skud.
Først da han nærmede sig Bagration, lod Rostov hesten gå i galop igen, og med hånden til salut red han op til generalen.
Dolgorukov insisterede stadig på, at franskmændene havde trukket sig tilbage og kun havde tændt bål for at narre os.
»Hvad beviser det?« sagde han, da Rostov red op. »De kan have trukket sig tilbage og efterladt forposterne.«
»Det er tydeligt, at de ikke alle er taget af sted endnu, fyrste,« sagde Bagration. »Vent til i morgen, så finder vi ud af alt i morgen.«

»Forposterne er stadig på bakken, Deres eksellence, præcis hvor de var i aftes,« rapporterede Rostov, bøjet forover med hånden til salut og ude af stand til at undertrykke det smil af glæde, som hans ridt og især lyden af kuglerne havde fremkaldt.
»Meget godt, meget godt,« sagde Bagration. »Tak, officer.«
»Deres eksellence,« sagde Rostov, »må jeg bede om en tjeneste?«
»Hvad er det?«
»I morgen skal vores eskadron være i reserven. Må jeg bede om at blive knyttet til den første eskadron?«
»Hvad hedder De?«
»Greve Rostov.«
»Åh, udmærket, De kan blive i min tjeneste.«
»Grev Ilja Rostovs søn?« spurgte Dolgorukov.
Men Rostov svarede ikke.
»Så kan jeg regne med det, Deres eksellence?«
»Jeg giver ordren.«
»I morgen bliver jeg måske sendt med en besked til kejseren,« tænkte Rostov.
»Gud ske lov!«

Bålene og råbene i den fjendtlige lejr skyldtes det faktum, at mens Napoleons proklamation blev oplæst for tropperne, red kejseren selv rundt om sine bivuakker. Soldaterne tændte halmviske, da de så ham, og løb efter ham med råbet: »Vive l'Empereur!« Napoleons proklamation lød som følger:

Soldater! Den russiske hær rykker frem mod jer for at hævne den østrigske hær fra Ulm. Det er de samme bataljoner, I slog ved Hollabrünn, og som I siden har forfulgt til dette sted. De stillinger, vi indtager, er stærke, og mens de marcherer for at gå uden om mig til højre, vil de blotte en flanke for mig. Soldater! Jeg vil selv lede jeres bataljoner. Jeg vil holde mig uden for ilden, hvis I med jeres vanlige tapperhed bringer uorden og forvirring i fjendens rækker; men skulle sejren et øjeblik være tvivlsom, vil I se jeres Kejser udsætte sig for de første fjendtlige kugler, for der må ikke herske tvivl om sejren, især ikke på denne dag, hvor det, der står på spil, er det franske infanteris ære, der er så nødvendig for vores nations ære.

Bryd ikke jeres rækker under påskud af at bortbære sårede! Lad enhver mand være gennemtrængt af den tanke, at vi må besejre disse Englands lejesoldater, drevet af et sådant had til vores nation! Denne sejr vil afslutte vores felttog, og vi kan vende tilbage til vinterkvarterer, hvor nye franske tropper, der nu udskrives i Frankrig, vil støde til os, og den fred, jeg vil slutte, vil være jeres, jeres folk og mig selv værdig.
NAPOLEON

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: That same night, Rostov was on skirmish duty with a platoon, positioned ahead of Bagration's detachment. His hussars were stationed along the line in pairs, and he rode back and forth trying to fight off the drowsiness that kept overcoming him. Behind him stretched an enormous space where the army's campfires glowed dimly through the fog; ahead was nothing but misty darkness. Rostov strained to see into that foggy distance but could make out nothing: now something seemed to gleam gray, now something looked black, now tiny lights appeared to flicker where the enemy should be, then he thought it might just be his own eyes playing tricks. His eyelids kept drooping, and in his half-dreams he saw the Emperor, then Denisov, then memories of Moscow — and then he'd jerk his eyes open again to see the head and ears of his horse right in front of him, and sometimes, when he rode within six paces, the dark shapes of hussars nearby. But in the distance, the same misty darkness remained. "Why not?" thought Rostov. "It could easily happen. The Emperor might come across me and give me an order, just like he would any other officer. He'd say: 'Go find out what's out there.' There are plenty of stories about him noticing an officer by chance and taking him onto his personal staff. What if he gave me a place at his side? Oh, how I would protect him, how I would tell him the truth, how I would expose the people deceiving him!" And to make his devoted love for the sovereign feel more vivid, Rostov imagined an enemy or a treacherous German whom he would not only kill with pleasure but slap across the face right in front of the Emperor. Suddenly a distant shout jerked him awake. He started and opened his eyes.

"Where am I? Oh, right — the skirmish line. Password and countersign: shaft, Olmutz. What a shame our squadron's in reserve tomorrow," he thought. "I'll ask for leave to go to the front. This might be my only chance to see the Emperor. It won't be long until my duty's over. I'll make one more round, and when I get back I'll go to the general and ask." He adjusted himself in the saddle and urged his horse forward to ride another circuit past his hussars. It seemed to him that the sky was growing lighter. To the left he could see an illuminated slope, and facing it a dark hill that looked steep as a wall. On this hill there was a white patch that Rostov couldn't identify — was it a moonlit clearing in the woods, unmelted snow, or some white buildings? He even thought he saw something move on that white spot. "Probably snow... a spot... a patch — une tache," he thought. "Wait... it's not a patch... Natasha... my sister, those dark eyes... Na-tasha... (Won't she be amazed when I tell her I saw the Emperor?) Natasha... take my sabretache..." — "Keep to the right, your honor, there are bushes here," came the voice of a hussar he was riding past, already half asleep. Rostov lifted his head, which had drooped almost to his horse's mane, and pulled up beside the hussar. He was surrendering to an irresistible, youthful, childlike drowsiness. "But what was I thinking about? I mustn't forget. How am I going to speak to the Emperor? No, that's not it — that's tomorrow. Oh yes! Natasha... sabretache... saber them... Whom? The hussars... Ah, the hussars with their mustaches. Down Tverskaya Street rode the hussar with the mustache... I was thinking about him too, right across from Guryev's house... Old Guryev... Oh, but Denisov's a wonderful fellow. But that's all nonsense. The main thing is that the Emperor is here. The way he looked at me and wanted to say something but didn't dare... No, it was I who didn't dare. But that's all nonsense — the main thing is not to forget the important thought I was having. Yes, Na-tasha, sabretache, oh yes, yes! That's right!" And his head sank to his horse's neck once more. Suddenly he thought he was being shot at. "What? What? What?... Cut them down! What?" said Rostov, jolting awake. The moment he opened his eyes, he heard from ahead — from the enemy's direction — the long, drawn-out shouts of thousands of voices. His horse and the hussar's horse beside him pricked up their ears at the sound. Over where the shouting came from, a fire flared up and then went out, then another, and then all along the French line on the hill, fires blazed up one after another and the shouting grew louder and louder. Rostov could hear French words but couldn't make them out. The roar of so many voices was too great; all he could distinguish was "ahahah!" and "rrrr!"
"What's going on? What do you think that is?" said Rostov to the hussar beside him. "That must be the enemy's camp!"
The hussar didn't reply.
"Well? Don't you hear it?" Rostov asked again, after waiting for an answer.
"Who can say, your honor?" the hussar replied reluctantly.
"From the direction, it has to be the enemy," Rostov repeated.
"Maybe it is, maybe it's nothing," the hussar muttered. "It's dark... Steady!" he called to his restless horse.

Rostov's horse was getting agitated too, pawing at the frozen ground, pricking its ears at the noise, and staring toward the lights. The shouting grew even louder, merging into a roar that only an army of several thousand men could produce. The lights spread farther along what was probably the French camp's line. Rostov no longer felt sleepy. The jubilant, triumphant shouting from the enemy camp had an electrifying effect on him. "Long live the Emperor! The Emperor!" — he could now hear the words distinctly.
"They can't be far away — probably just beyond the stream," he said to the hussar beside him.

The hussar only sighed, said nothing, and coughed irritably. The sound of hooves approaching at a trot along the line of hussars reached them, and out of the foggy darkness the figure of a hussar sergeant appeared, looming as large as an elephant.
"Your honor, the generals!" said the sergeant, riding up to Rostov.

Rostov, still glancing back toward the fires and the shouting, rode with the sergeant to meet some mounted men coming along the line. One of them was on a white horse. It was Prince Bagration and Prince Dolgorukov, with their adjutants, who had come to see the strange spectacle of lights and shouts from the enemy camp for themselves. Rostov rode up to Bagration, made his report, and then joined the adjutants listening to the generals' conversation.
"Believe me," said Prince Dolgorukov, turning to Bagration, "it's nothing but a ruse. He's retreated and left fires and noise behind to fool us."

"I doubt it," said Bagration. "I saw them on that hill this evening. If they'd retreated, they would have pulled out from there too... Officer!" he said to Rostov. "Are the enemy's skirmishers still in position?"
"They were there this evening, but I can't say for certain now, your excellency. Shall I ride out with some of my hussars to check?" Rostov replied.
Bagration stopped and tried to make out Rostov's face through the mist before answering.
"Well, go and see," he said after a pause.
"Yes, sir."

Rostov spurred his horse, called Sergeant Fedchenko and two other hussars, told them to follow, and trotted downhill toward the source of the shouting. He felt both scared and excited to be riding alone with three hussars into that mysterious, dangerous, misty unknown where no one had gone before him. Bagration called after him from the hilltop not to cross the stream, but Rostov pretended not to hear and kept riding on, continually mistaking bushes for trees and ditches for men, and continually realizing his mistakes. After descending the hill at a trot, he could no longer see either the Russian or the French campfires, but he heard the French shouting more loudly and clearly. In the valley ahead he saw what looked like a river, but when he reached it, he found it was a road. Coming out onto the road, he reined in his horse, hesitating whether to follow it or cross it and ride up the black hillside. Staying on the road, which gleamed white through the mist, would have been safer — easier to spot people coming. "Follow me!" he said. He crossed the road and began galloping uphill toward where the French pickets had been posted that evening.

"Your honor, there he is!" cried one of the hussars behind him. And before Rostov could make out what the dark shape in the fog was, there was a flash, a report, and a bullet whizzed high overhead through the mist with a mournful whine and passed out of hearing. Another musket misfired but flashed in the pan. Rostov wheeled his horse around and galloped back. Four more shots rang out at intervals, the bullets whistling past somewhere in the fog, each with a different pitch. Rostov eased his horse to a walk — the animal's spirits had risen with the firing, just like his own — and headed back at a leisurely pace. "More! Come on, more!" a happy voice said inside him. But no more shots came.
Only when he was close to Bagration did Rostov let his horse gallop again, and he rode up to the general with his hand at the salute.
Dolgorukov was still insisting that the French had retreated and had only left fires behind to trick them.
"What does that prove?" he was saying as Rostov rode up. "They could retreat and leave the pickets."
"It's clear they haven't all gone, Prince," said Bagration. "Let's wait until tomorrow morning — we'll find out everything then."

"The picket is still on the hill, your excellency — right where it was this evening," Rostov reported, leaning forward with his hand at the salute, unable to suppress the smile of exhilaration that his ride and especially the sound of the bullets had produced.
"Very good, very good," said Bagration. "Thank you, officer."
"Your excellency," said Rostov, "may I ask a favor?"
"What is it?"
"Our squadron is supposed to be in reserve tomorrow. May I request to be attached to the first squadron?"
"What's your name?"
"Count Rostov."
"Oh, very well — you may remain in my personal retinue."
"Count Ilya Rostov's son?" asked Dolgorukov.
But Rostov didn't reply.
"Then I can count on it, your excellency?"
"I'll give the order."
"Tomorrow I might even be sent with a message to the Emperor," Rostov thought.
"Thank God!"

The fires and shouting in the enemy camp were caused by the fact that Napoleon's proclamation was being read to the troops, and the Emperor himself was riding through his bivouacs. The soldiers, catching sight of him, lit bundles of straw and ran after him shouting, "Long live the Emperor!" Napoleon's proclamation read as follows:

Soldiers! The Russian army is advancing against you to avenge the Austrian army of Ulm. These are the same battalions you crushed at Hollabrunn and have been chasing ever since. The position we hold is a strong one, and while they march to outflank me on the right, they will expose their flank. Soldiers! I will personally direct your battalions. I will stay out of the firing line if, with your customary bravery, you carry chaos and confusion into the enemy's ranks. But should victory be in doubt even for a moment, you will see your Emperor expose himself to the enemy's first blows, for there must be no uncertainty about victory — especially on this day, when the honor of the French infantry is at stake, so vital to the honor of our nation.

Do not break ranks on the excuse of helping the wounded! Let every man be filled with the conviction that we must defeat these mercenaries of England, who harbor such hatred for our nation! This victory will end our campaign, and we can return to winter quarters where fresh French troops being raised in France will join us. The peace I will then make will be worthy of my people, of you, and of myself.
NAPOLEON
